en: Now, the supplement to the Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī; now begins the section on the treatment of bile diseases (pitta-roga). 1.
Having respectfully prostrated before the scholar Sātyanārāyaṇa, who upholds the truth,
I compose this *Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī*.
This is the remainder of what was desired to be explained. ||1||
First among those [diseases] are the disorders of bile (pitta):
premature graying of the hair, redness of the eyes, redness of the urine, yellowness of the eyes, and likewise yellowness of the urine. (1)
The yellowness of the stool is declared [as a sign], as well as the yellowness of the nails, the yellowness of the teeth, and likewise of the body. (2)
There is also a vision of darkness and a perception of everything as yellow;
there is little sleep and so forth, dryness in the mouth, and a metallic taste. (3)
There is also bitterness in the mouth as well as acidity of the face;
moreover, there is heat in the breath and likewise the belching of smoke.

Delusion, fatigue, as well as anger, burning heat accompanied by a sense of internal division, the impairment of the vital energy, the desire for cold, lack of contentment, and likewise restlessness; ||5||
There is a burning sensation after eating, sharpness of the digestive fire, discharge of blood, diarrhea, and likewise heat in the stool. (6)
There is heat in the urine, difficulty in urination, scantiness of semen, thinness and heat of the body, a foul odor of the sweat, as well as the peeling away of the skin. ||7||

Lassitude of the body and likewise suppuration of the physique—these forty are considered by the sages to be the diseases of pitta. The treatment for these should be understood by the wise in their respective sections. 8.
For *dhātrīlauha*, one should take eight *palas* of *dhātrī* powder, four *palas* of iron powder, and two *palas* of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* powder; these should be rubbed on a cloth. (9)
This powder should be kept with *amṛtā* decoction for seven days;
having been thoroughly dried in the fierce sun, it should be ground again and placed in a new jar. (10)
One should always eat this three times a day—mixed with ghee and honey—at the beginning, middle, and end of the meal; it is wholesome according to the persistence of the humors. ||11||
At the beginning of a meal, it destroys disorders caused by pitta;
in the middle, it removes abdominal distension and constipation; and at the end, it cures the dullness of the digestive fire.
It undoubtedly destroys diseases arising from raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders). ||12||
Equal parts of pittāntakara, nutmeg, cardamom, jasmine fruit, māṃsī, kuṣṭha, tālīśapatra, honey, dead iron, and divine mica [are to be taken]. (13)
Having ground together equal parts of mercury and silver with water, one should prepare pills weighing two guñjas; these destroy diseases of the bile. 14.
The pitta located in the visceral cavities (koṣṭha) as well as that situated in the peripheral tissues (śākhā),
it quickly destroys colic, acid gastritis (amlapitta), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), chlorosis (halīmaka), hemorrhoids (durnāma), and vertigo (bhrānti).
For this is a medicinal preparation that destroys pitta, as proclaimed by the King of Kāśī. ||16||
This is the Mahāpittāntakara rasa; if, having omitted honey, gold is added here, it is named Mahāpittāntaka, which destroys all types of pitta. ||17||

In the case of a disease of *pitta*, the wholesome regimen consists of drinking clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), purgation (*virecana*), emesis (*vamana*), and the administration of honey; white rice, barley, wheat, and grass-grains (*tṛṇadhānyaka*); chickpeas (*caṇaka*), green gram (*mudga*), lentils (*masūra*), and barley (*yava*);
thin gruel (*maṇḍa*), aged water, and milks; as well as sugar-cane juice, honey, and *mākṣika* honey.
Parched grain, the juices of desert plants, clarified butters, sugar, cold water, and the water from the Udbhida well.
Karkoṭa, plantain, thorny fruit, the tip of a cane, māṣāḍhaka, grapes, kulaka, very tender kūṣmāṇḍa,
ervārūka, gourd, parpaṭaka, the leaf of alpamāriṣa, kāṭhillaka, and pomegranate—
The *dhātrī*, the tender *tāla* fruit, the *abhayā*, the *kharjūra*, and the *audumbara*. ||19||
One should also consume pomegranate, along with astringent, bitter, and sweet substances; madhūka, varī, bronze, iron, silver, gold, kaṭukā, nimba, trivṛt, and sandalwood.
One should frequent palatial mansions, underground chambers, very cool groves, fountain-houses, moonlight, plantains, lotuses, beds of fresh leaves, cold plasters, and cooling applications. (20)
Sleeping on the ground, jewels, the time of twilight, the embrace of a beloved, bathing, meeting with friends, pleasant conversation, gentle breezes,
sprinkling with water, listening to musical instruments, and the sight of graceful dancing— these are the states that are most agreeable to the mind.
And the flowers of the punnāga, utpala, pāṭala, abja, sumana, and kalhāra. ||21||
Camphor, water from the riverbank, all cooling procedures, and this regimen of drink, food, recreation, and medicine—when adopted, will bring about the pacification of pitta. ||22||

In the case of a disease of *pitta*, the following are unwholesome: smoking, sudation, exposure to the sun, sexual intercourse, suppression of natural urges, anger, alkaline substances, travel, improper riding on elephants or horses, sharp medical procedures, physical exercise,
foods that cause a burning sensation in the mouth, the summer season, and the consumption of incompatible foods.
Midday, the passing of the clouds, midnight, and middle age—these are all [times of transition]. (23)
Rice, barley grain, sesame, garlic, black gram, horse gram, jaggery, flat beans, liquor, linseed, cow’s urine, water, fermented rice-gruel,
warm water, citron, water lily-root decoction, asafoetida, breadfruit, various urines, marking-nut, betel leaf, curd, mustard, jujube, oil-drinking, and tamarind— [these are the purgatives]. (24)
Bitter, sour, salty, and burning—this regimen of drink, food, recreation, and medicine has been firmly determined by the foremost physicians to be poison in the provocation of Pitta. (25)
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of bile diseases in the Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī-pariśiṣṭa. 1.
Now follows the supplement to the *Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī*, namely, Chapter Two: The Section on the Treatment of Diseases of Kapha.
At the beginning of that [season], diseases of phlegm arise first: sweetness in the mouth, as well as a coating sensation in the mouth, excessive salivation, and likewise an excess of sleep. (1)
A gurgling sound in the throat, a bitter longing for pungent and hot things, dullness of intellect, lack of consciousness, laziness, and even satiety [arise]. (2)
Sluggishness of the digestive fire, an excess of waste products, and likewise the whiteness of those wastes;
an excess of urine, the whiteness of the urine, and likewise an excess of semen. (3)
Stiffness, heaviness, and coldness— these twenty, through their combination and manifestation, are declared by the sages to be the diseases of phlegm (ślaiṣmika).
The specific treatment for each of these should be understood by the wise in their respective sections. ||5||
Methods for pacifying kapha:
For kapha, having accumulated during the cold season, is heated by the rays of the sun in spring;
it destroys the digestive fire and produces diseases here and there—therefore, one should employ [remedies] accordingly. (6)
Strong emetics and nasal therapies, gargles and collyriums, physical exercise, dry massage, medicinal smoking, and lukewarm water for acts of cleansing; ||7||
For the purpose of dispelling the provocation of phlegm (kapha), the excellent service of fire is prescribed, as well as emesis, nasal medication (nasya), and the consumption of dry substances. 8.
Sexual pleasure, physical exertion, and exposure to the wind are beneficial;
pungent, alkaline, and sour substances should be consumed as a purifying treatment when [the disease] arises from phlegm (kapha). 9.
Take equal parts of hiṅgula, indrayava, ṭaṅkaṇa, trailokyabīja, and marica; then add three parts of sūtabhasma (mercury ash). This is the Kaphacintāmaṇi-rasa. ||10||
One should grind ginger with its own juice for exactly one prahara;
it quickly destroys diseases of phlegm, just as the sun destroys darkness. ||11||
Take an abundant quantity of Kaphaketurasa, equal parts of pearl and gold, and an amount of coral ash equal to those two;
then add double the amount of coral of abhra (mica). One may optionally substitute the essence of sindūra for the gold. 12.
This should be diligently ground with milk in a vessel of white stone by skilled physicians;
one desiring the immediate destruction of phlegm should consume three *guñjā* seeds of this when there is an aggravation of *kapha*. 13.
The Mahāśleṣmakāsānalarasa consists of mercury derived from cinnabar (hiṅgula), realgar, sulphur, borax, copper,
tin, mica, gold-oxide (svarṇākṣika), and talc. ||14||
Dhūstūra, Saindhava salt, Kuṣṭha, Pippalī, Hiṅgu, Kaṭphala, Dantī seeds, Somarājī, Vanarājaphala, and Trivṛt. ||15||
The physician should prepare pills by thoroughly mixing [the powder] with the milky sap of the Vajrī plant; one should consume a single pill, the size of a pea, according to one's strength. ||16||
It quickly destroys a combination [of humors], just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree, or as a rutting lion in the forest is the destroyer of the herds of deer. ||17||
Likewise, this great [mantra] is the immediate destroyer of all diseases. 18.
The essence of the king of mountains (śilājatu), mercury, sulphur, iron, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the two types of cumin,
śaṭī, śṛṅgī, yamānī, pauṣkara, and likewise ginger; ||19||
Red ochre, barley-ash, borax, elephant pepper, jasmine bud, ajamoda, varā, yavāsa, and cloves; ||20||
Take one *tolaka* each of the seeds of *kanaka*, *ārūṇa*, *kaṭphala*, and *cavyaka*, and have them ground into a fine powder. (21)
Having rubbed it with stone hammers upon a clean stone mortar,
one should add the juice of bilva roots along with arka, citraka, and triphalā.
Nirguṇḍī, gaṇikā, vāsā, indrāśana, pracodanī, dhustūra, kṛṣṇājīra, pippalī, and pāribhadraka. ||23||
One should rub these with their juices and process them with fresh ginger;
taken with a post-digestive drink of warm water, it destroys all diseases. (24)

[It cures] the twenty diseases arising from phlegm (śleṣman), ailments born of the combination of humors (saṃnipāta), the eight types of abdominal enlargements (udarāṣṭaka), hemorrhoids (durnāma), and the terrible āmavāta. ||25||
It destroys the five defects of the body and worms, as well as obesity in men;
it increases the digestive fire just as fire increases when fed with dry fuel. 26.
One should cook mustard oil with the decoction and paste of *dhustūra*;
it cures fever caused by the derangement of all three humors (*saṃnipāta*), phlegm disorders, coldness, headache, and burning sensations.
It removes the seizing pain of the ears and destroys stiffness in the joints of the bones. ||27||
Kanakataila, kanakārka, balā, dūrvā, vāsaka, vaijayantikā, nirguṇḍī, pūtikā, bhārgī, koṭhaka, and punarnavā. ||28||
The leaf of *badarī*, *vijayā*, *śrīphala*, as well as *bṛhatī*, *citraka*, the root of *snuhī*, *agnimantha*, and *vyaḍambaka*— 29.
One should take two palas each of bṛhadbhaṇḍī, māgadhī, and the leaf of āragvadha; this should be done at that very moment.
One drona of water should be boiled down until only one-fourth remains;
then, one prastha of pungent mustard seeds should be cooked over a fierce fire.
One should administer all these substances ground into a paste for the relief of eye pain, headache, and elephantiasis arising from the flesh and blood.
It undoubtedly destroys rheumatism (āmavāta), pain in the heart, enlargement of the scrotum, goiter, swelling, deafness, abdominal disease, and cough. ||33||
When a drop falls upon dūrvā grass, it becomes dry at that very moment;
this oil, named Kanaka, is the destroyer of the family of kapha and skin eruptions. 34.
In diseases of *kapha*, the wholesome regimen consists of emesis,
fasting, collyrium, sexual intercourse, vigorous massage, sudation, anxiety, staying awake, physical exertion, excessive walking, and the suppression of the urge to urinate.

Gargling, rubbing [the teeth], blowing [into the nose], the management of elephants, horses, and vehicles, medicinal smoke, fanning, wrestling, excessive agitation, nasal medication, and fear [are contraindications for errhines]. ||35||
Rough and hot dietary preparations from previous lives; *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, *niṣpāva* beans, grass-grains, chickpeas, mung beans, horse-gram, and barley;
alkaline substances, mustard oil, warm water, the meat of desert animals, black mustard;
the tips of cane, *kulaka*, the fruit of *kaṭhillaka*, eggplant, and *audumbara* fruit. (36)

Karkoṭa, garlic, the flower of the Moca tree, Śakrāśana, Śūraṇa, Nimba, Mūlakāpotikā, Varuṇa, bitter [herbs], Trivṛt, honey, betel leaf, water infused with Nalada, aged wine, the three pungents (vyoṣa), Chebulic myrobalan, cow’s urine, parched grain, rice prepared with excellent ghee, and a comfortably warm dwelling place. ||37||
Bell-metal, iron, collyrium, pearls, bitter garments, and astringent tastes—this regimen of drink, food, conduct, and medicine shall conquer even virulent phlegm. (38)

In diseases of *kapha*, unwholesome [factors] include: oleation, anointing, sitting during the day, sleeping, bathing, eating incompatible foods, the forenoon, the cold season, the springtime, the beginning of the night, and the first stage of life.
And at the beginning of a meal, one should avoid new grain, new drinks, fresh black gram, rice, fish, meat, molasses, milk products, and the liquid extracted from the marrow of palmyra seeds. (39)
Rice gruel, upodikā, jackfruit, mushrooms, māṣāḍhaka, dates, ointments, milk, petīya, and milk-rice— these,
as well as what is sweet, sour, salty, heavy, cold, and satiating, are recommended.
In the provocation of phlegm (śleṣman), this—consisting of drink, food, lifestyle, and medicine—is poison. 40.
Thus ends the second chapter, on the treatment of diseases caused by *kapha*, in the Appendix of the *Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī*.
Now follows the supplement to the Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī;
here begins the section on experienced formulations (Anubhūta-yoga). 3.
Now, all those formulations experienced by the venerable Rājeśvara Śāstrin—both ancient and new—are being written down for the delight of physicians. (1)
To remove the fever of men (in cases of new fever), one should grind mercury, copper, trivṛt, bala, tikta, dantī seeds, capalā, viṣatindu,
and pathyā in equal parts, and take them with golden water for one day. ||2||
A pill made from two parts of *vallī* and one part of *vaṭikā*, taken on a Monday, will quickly destroy a fresh fever.
In this matter of removing the affliction of the world, the wholesome diet consists of light meals accompanied by mung beans and *śaṣa*. ||3||
In the case of fever caused by vāta and pitta,

one should powder together mercury, cinnabar, viṣa, vyoṣa, ṭaṅkaṇa, and the root of māgadhī; then, having powdered them, one should saturate the mixture three times with the juices of *surasā*, *ārdraka*, and gold.
The juice known as Tribhuvanakīrtti, when combined with the fresh juice of Guñjā, indeed destroys all fevers and the thirteen types of saṃnipāta. ||5||
In cases of Pitta-fever, internal burning, and thirst, [the decoction] beginning with sandalwood is used;
likewise, white sandalwood and excellent red sandalwood, as well as parpaṭa, coriander, neem root-bark, and padmaka [are employed]. (6)
Kirātatikta, uśīra, mahāśrāvaṇikā, bṛhadelā, and taruṇīkusuma, each separately. ||7||
One part of guḍūcī and two parts of [the other ingredient], both finely ground together, should be boiled in sixteen times their quantity of water for four watches (sixteen hours). 8.
Having carefully placed it [therein], the eminent physician should protect it from the crane-trap mechanism and extract the clear juice according to the prescribed rule. 9.
In cases of internal burning, thirst, and fever arising from pitta, this Arkacandana compound should indeed be administered in the appropriate dosage. 10.
Regarding the treatment for fever caused by kapha and pitta (Tiktāvaṭī):
One should prepare pills the size of a pea by impregnating the powder of Tiktā with the juice extracted from the leaves of Kāravella. (11)
Then, with devotion, one should take two pills in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, using water that is measured by a mouthful and is lukewarm. ||12||
When this has been done, the patient suffering from fever caused by phlegm and bile shall become comfortable; thus it was declared by the Lord of the King of Physicians. 13.

In the case of *saptaparṇasattvādivaṭī* (for irregular fever), take equal parts of the essence derived from *saptaparṇa*, the essence of *kaṭukā*, the essence of *kupīlu*, and the essence derived from *yavatiktā*. (14)

Each substance, weighing ten *tolakas*, should be taken by those who know the materia medica; the wise man should carefully grind everything together until it is equal to the total weight of the powder. 15.
The physician should then mix the marrow of the *karañja* seed therein; all of this should subsequently be ground together with water in a mortar. 16.
Pills should be prepared resembling black gram (kalāya) and dried in the shade;
one pill or two pills should be administered according to necessity. 17.
Should it be taken three or four times daily with warm water, or rather, with plain water alone, by one suffering from intermittent fever with joy? (18)
This auspicious pill, consisting of *saptaparṇa*, *sattva*, and other ingredients, has been described by the best of physicians for the purpose of destroying irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*). 19.
The powder of Bilva and others (for dysentery with undigested matter):
a paste of Bilva, Bhaṅgā, purified Viśuddhā, Mahauṣadha, Dhātrī flowers, and Dhānyaka—all these in equal parts. (20)
One should especially take a fourth part of śatapuṣpā;
having gathered all of this together, one should have it made into a fine powder.
This powder made from bilva and other ingredients is quickly and completely beneficial;
it is the supreme refuge for those suffering from dysentery and diarrhea. 22.
From four māṣakas up to six māṣakas here daily, two or three times, according to necessity, with joy. (23)
"It may be taken with water or with rice-water mixed with a gadī (a small measure);
thus spoke the wise King of Physicians, the Lord of Kings. (24)
The powder of *dhātakī* and other ingredients (for diarrhea and dysentery): one part of *dhātakī* flowers, an equal amount of *rasa* (resin) derived from *sarja*,
and two parts of sugar— all these together.
Then, having ground it finely, one should purify it with a cloth. ||25||
The powder known as Dhātakī-ādi quickly destroys diarrhea and dysentery;
its dose should be one, two, or three māṣakas, taken twice or thrice daily. (26)
For cholera (visūcikā) and diarrhea (atisāra),
the physician should add thirty seṭakas of water and five tolakas of camphor, and then let it ferment according to the prescribed method for one week. (27)
One should carefully preserve it in a jar; then, having purified it with a cloth, one should give it likewise to one suffering from dysentery or one afflicted by visūcī (intestinal obstruction). 28.
One should bestow this sacred learning in the world like camphor-water, according to one's capacity, beginning from two tolas up to five tolas. (29)
The dosage should be determined by carefully observing the patient, the disease, and its constant manifestations;
this has been experienced many times by physicians who are well-versed in the scriptures. (30)
Regarding the fumigation for hemorrhoids (*arśas*):
one should grind together in equal parts rotten *pūgī* fruit, coconut, and *viṣatinduka* grown along the river. (31)
By this very method, the alleviation of pain occurs through fumigation for hemorrhoids;
this is the hemorrhoid-destroying smoke (ārśoghna-dhūma) approved by the physicians of King Īśvara. ||32||
One part of the marrow of the great nimba (mahanimba), as well as one part of the fruit-marrow of the nimba;
two parts of rasāñjana [should be taken]. (33)
One part of the powder of the *tṛṇakānta* gem, and specifically one part of *raktabola*; having carefully collected all of this together—34.
The best of physicians should grind it with water in the middle of a mortar;
then, he should prepare pills the size of a guñjā fruit. ||35||
One should administer one or two pills with water every day for blood hemorrhoids, either twice or thrice, as appropriate. ||36||
Thus ends the pill named Arśoghnī Vaṭī, which brings relief to hemorrhoidal bleeding, as spoken by Śrī Rājeśvaradatta, the son of Vādya-raja. 37.
In the treatment of hemorrhoids (arśoroga),
one *seṭaka* measure of cow's ghee processed a hundred times (*śatadhautaghṛta*) and ten *karṣas* of the excellent essence of *candrapodīkā* [are required]. (38)
Likewise, having taken five karṣas each of yavānikā and satva, first place them into the substance produced from yavānī and podikā. (39)

One should place all these ingredients, including camphor, in equal proportions into a glass flask until they reach a liquid state; then, having carefully sealed its mouth, one should set it aside for a fortnight. (40)
Once all that has been liquefied, the wise and best of physicians, having added ghee washed a hundred times, should set it aside. 41.
It is proclaimed to provide immediate relief to one afflicted by the pain of hemorrhoids, and it is also said to cause the extreme contraction of swollen hemorrhoids. 42.
This remedy, experienced by Rājeśvara and known by the name Arśovedanāntaka, should be applied by those afflicted with hemorrhoids, who are filled with joy and free from doubt. 43.
Rūkmiśa rasa (for hemorrhoids with blood, constipation, and obstruction):
Taking powdered Abhayā mixed with fresh Jayapāla seeds in a one-fifth proportion, they should be ground together with the milky sap of Snuhī. ||44||
Pills should be made from each of these minerals, along with purgatives and juices, round and the size of chickpeas. 45.
In cases of jaundice (rūkṣiṇ), there shall be no burning sensation, nor fainting, giddiness, or exhaustion;
this [medicine] purges with force and especially destroys abdominal distension. 46.
Neither by a decoction enema (nirūha), nor by bindu-ghṛta, nor by trivṛt is one purged as effectively as by this supreme pill (guḍikā). 47.
The body shall indeed become exceedingly pure, most powerful, and excellent; it shall possess supreme beauty, be highly mature, and grant an excellent lifespan. 48.
In cases of constipation, a pill should be administered;
in the case of severe abdominal disease, the great medicine (mahauṣadhi) is given in all the lower regions and in the rectum.
It is administered and then digested, subduing the āma and increasing the power of the body at will. ||49||
In the *Cikitsādarśa*, regarding the treatment of indigestion (*arkavaṭī*):
the dried bark of the root of the *arka* plant should be finely ground into powder; to an amount equal to that [powder], one should add black pepper and rock salt (*saindhava*) separately. (50)
Having collected even the pulverized [substance] and rubbed it with the juice of *nimbū*, one should form pills the size of chickpeas according to the prescribed rite every hour. (51)
"However, one whose mind is fearful of indigestion should resort [to food] with a desire for health"—this counsel of good physicians King Rājeśvarabudha experienced. (52)
The Arkapuṣpādi Vaṭikā (for sluggish digestion and abdominal pain):
pure marrow derived from the Arkapuṣpa plant, pure asafoetida,
pure *rupīluka*, and pure *narasāraka* [53].
Having taken black pepper and ground it into equal parts, one should grind everything with water and form a pill resembling black pepper in appearance. (54)
Having prepared it with great care, one should protect it with water that is neither too cold nor too hot;
indeed, for abdominal ailments, one should apply one or two small pieces [of the medicine] upon a pointed rod.
Therefore, the best of physicians should especially employ these [remedies] in cases of diminished digestive fire;
because they have been experienced by me constantly, they are revealed in this treatise. (56)
In the case of both indigestion (agnimāndya) and colic (śūlaroga), take three parts of *kuberākṣavaṭī*, three parts of the marrow of *karañja*,
three parts of *trikaṭu*, and likewise one part of *sauvarcala* salt. (57)
Having ground all these together into a powder, one should triturate them with water;
then, pills measuring two raktis each should be prepared according to the prescribed method. 58.
This Kuberākṣavaṭī, when consumed with warm water, destroys severe dullness of the digestive fire as well as colic arising from the abdomen. (59)
The dosage of this should be administered by the practitioner as one pill or two pills, twice or thrice daily, according to the patient's capacity. (60)
Regarding the powder of the essence of *amlikā* and other ingredients (for the treatment of flatulence):
the portion derived from the essence of *amlikā* shall be one-fifth of the total; that produced from the essence of *podikā* is declared to be one forty-eighth part. (61)
Two parts of coriander, one part derived from cumin, and one part each of ginger and *śatapuṣpā*, taken separately. (62)
Having gathered all these together, one should have them made into a fine powder; then, having mixed them, one should preserve them in a glass jar according to the prescribed rule. 63.
This powder, consisting of *amlīkā* and other substances in their complete form, quickly destroys flatulence and especially produces a relish for food. 64.
It is known as the supreme digestive stimulant that kindles the gastric fire;
here, excellent physicians should recognize lukewarm water as the appropriate after-drink (anupāna). 65.
The powder of Madhuyaṣṭyādi (for mild purgation):
Madhuyaṣṭi should be two parts, and svarṇapattrī likewise;
so too should śatapuṣpā, dāru, niśā, and purified sulphur. (66)
Each [of the other ingredients] should be one part, while the sugar should measure seven parts;
having ground everything together into a single mass, one should have it drunk with warm milk.
A powder measured at six māṣakas bestows beauty upon the teeth and acts as a mild purgative;
this has been especially experienced by Śāstrī Rājeśvara. (68)

For a mild purgative, the powder of black seeds (kṛṣṇabīja) and other ingredients should be used; the black seeds, well-fried, constitute eight parts as the best portion, four parts of gold-leaf (svarṇapatra), and two parts of dry ginger (nāgara). (69)
One part of śatapuṣpā and likewise the flower of taruṇī—having ground all this together and then filtered it through a cloth. ||70||
There, one should carefully mix in a portion of sugar equal to one-eighth of the [other] ingredients,
having processed it according to the prescribed method with the juice of citron.
Having prepared the dried dust by rubbing it according to the prescribed method,
one who knows the ritual should preserve that powder of black seeds and other ingredients in a glass vessel.
From three māṣakas up to six māṣakas, when taken with water, this is a mild digestive and purgative for those afflicted by disease. (73)
The powder of six ingredients consists of four parts of svarṇapatrī, two parts of a small amount of śivā,
and one part each of sauvarcala, saindhava, śuṇṭhī, and śatapuṣpikā. (74)
Each [ingredient] should be one part, and one should grind them all together into a powder;
this six-ingredient powder (ṣaṭsākara) should always be measured at six māṣakas. ||75||
Having been treated with warm water, this is supremely beneficial, providing comfort and excellent purgation;
this has been tested extensively by the masters of the scriptures. (76)
For the treatment of catarrh (pratiśyāya),
take three *māṣa* each of *vanapsikā* and other astringents (*kaṣāya*), as well as *vanapsikā* flowers, *gojihvā*, *madhuka*, and *khaṭamī*. (77)
Likewise, there were seeds of the Śleṣmātaka tree numbering ten (the directions), and all the seeds of the Unnābaka tree, which were half that number. 78.
Having combined these together in one place, boil them in a kuḍava of water;
once you have determined that half remains, strain it through a cloth. ||79||
Having added sugar to that, one should drink it while it is comfortably warm;
this is declared to be the decoction known as Vanaspatyādi. ||80||
This application for the pacification of catarrh is unsurpassed;
it has been tested in many ways by the lords of physicians and kings. (81)
For asthma,
the smoke [should be prepared] with *kṣudrā* seeds, *kānaka* leaves dried in the shade,
*yavānikā*, *pārasīkayavānī*, *soraka*, and *niśā*. (82)
The physician should take the entire contents of the jar in equal portions according to the prescribed rule; he should then carefully set aside a small portion of that [powder]. 83.
This was experienced continuously by Śāstrirājeśvara;
then, as the patient was despondent due to the extreme severity of the forceful breathing, [he intervened]. (84)
One should cause that smoke to be inhaled or smelled according to the prescribed method;
by this, the patient is immediately freed from the distress of asthma. 85.
Keśaravaṭī (for dyspnea and cough):
One *tolaka* of excellent Kashmiri saffron (*keśara*), two *tolakas* each of cardamom (*elā*) and *abhayā* (myrobalan) produced from *valuka*, [are to be taken]. (86)
Having ground all of this together with the juice of *taruṇī* flowers, auspicious pills the size of chickpeas should be prepared. (87)
This Keśaravaṭī should be taken with water; it brings relief from asthma and cough, acts as a mild purgative, and its dose is one pill. 88.
Or rather, should two pills be taken by the patient in the morning and evening?
This has been experienced by excellent physicians; no further deliberation is required here. (89)
In the treatment of wind disorders (vātavyādhi), one should take jyotiṣmatī weighing two and a half iṣṭakas, and yamānikā weighing fifty karṣas; this is the oil of suvarṇalatikā and others. (90)
One part each of ākārakarabha, methī, and lavaṅga, along with twenty-five karṣas of rasenaka, should be taken according to their respective measures. (91)
The physician should take one and a half seers of excellent red marica, prepare a paste of these according to the prescribed method, and set it aside. 92.
Taking two *tulās* each of a decoction of *taca* and *mūṣikaparṇī*, as well as *kaṭutaila* (mustard oil), one should cook them all together in a single vessel. (93)
Having recognized that the oil is cooked, one should purify it with a cloth;
this is the unsurpassed oil, such as Suvarṇalatikā and others. 94.
This is especially beneficial when consumed constantly in cases of Vātavyādhi (wind-related disorders);
thus is it generally the well-ascertained experience of physicians. ||95||
Apatantraka, harīvaṭī, karpūra, rāmaṭha, gañjā, and pārasīkayavānikā should be taken in portions of two, two, two, eight, two, and two [parts] respectively, according to the prescribed rule. 96.
The physician, having collected the powder in one place, should grind it with water;
in this preparation, asafoetida fried in cow's ghee is to be taken as the best ingredient. (97)
Pills measured by black pepper should be prepared with great care;
one auspicious pill should be consumed with water every morning and evening. 98.
This Vaṭī pill, known as Apatantraharī because it removes apatantraka, was both experienced and made famous by Śrī Rājeśvara Śāstrī. (99)

Yāvanaratneśvara (is effective) in cases of fainting, insanity, epilepsy, and heart-weakness; likewise, pearls, emeralds, coral, and topaz, when ground together and prepared according to the prescribed method, [are beneficial]. 100.
The physician, an enemy to disease, should take one *tolaka* each of *agnijāra*, *nirviṣa*, and *kauśayaja* powder. (101)
Powdered sky-stone (vyomāśman), the ash of a deer's horn, and very beautiful sea-nut (sāmudra) from a coconut—each [of these] should be four tolas. 102.
The physician should grind together one tola each of musk, silver, and excellent gold in the form of fine leaf-gold. 103.
Having thus processed it with effort for fourteen days according to the prescribed rite, using arka oil produced from tūraṇī flowers; 104.
Then, beautiful pills, each measuring one rakti, should be prepared;
they should be administered continuously according to the specific humors involved. 105.
This Ratneśvara is a Yavana; it is pleasing to the heart and especially strengthening, yet it always causes vertigo and a distressing throbbing of the heart. (106)
It removes [the poison], increases strength immediately, and destroys diseases such as insanity, fainting, and epilepsy. (107)
Increasing the intelligence of the wise, he indeed rejoiced thousands of times;
this one, known as Moharānta, has especially brought about the destruction of delusion today. 108.
It is prescribed in the medical treatises of the Yavanas and is employed by the most eminent physicians. ||109||
The iron preparation (lauha) beginning with *vṛddhadāru* [is used] for *āmavāta*;
this iron [compound], containing *vṛddhadāru*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *gajapippalī*, and *māṇaka*, combined with the three groups of three [pungent spices], is the destroyer of *āmavāta*. 110.
It destroys all diseases, just as a lion destroys elephants. ||111||
Mahānārāca Rasa (for the disease of Gulma):

One should grind together equal parts of copper, mercury, sulphur, *jaipāla*, the three fruits (*triphalā*), and *kaṭuka* with alkaline substances; one should drink a *niṣka* of this preparation to destroy gulma.
One should drink warm water afterwards; this Nārāca is a great elixir. ||112||
One should dissolve two parts of white parpaṭī (the root of śoraka) in water and cook it;
once it has been reduced and dissolved, one should strain it through a cloth. ||113||
Then, one should mix crystal (sphaṭikā) measuring half that portion therein;
it should be cooked again until it reaches a state of density. ||114||
Once density has been achieved, one should place it upon a plantain leaf, cover it with another leaf, and press it down with a heavy object. 115.
Then, having ascertained that it has become cool, the expert in medicine should separate it from that [mixture] and place it in a glass vessel. ||116||
Since its strength is like that of milk and it is indeed a parpaṭī, for that very reason it is called *śvetaparpaṭī* by physicians in the world. 117.
This [mixture] is exceedingly diuretic and never fails to work;
one should take cold water or sugar-water as an after-drink (anupāna) with it. ||118||
The Varuṇādyalauha (for mūtrakṛcchra):
two palas of varuṇa, half of that (one pala) of dhātrī, half a pala of dhātrī flowers, half a pala of harītakī, and half of that (one-quarter pala) of pṛśniparṇī. ||119||
One who knows the ritual procedure should grind iron and mica together into a powder and consume one *śāṇa* measure every morning after rising. (120)
It quickly destroys severe urinary obstruction, painful dysuria, urinary calculi, prameha, and irregular fever. 121.
This iron preparation beginning with Varuṇa, composed by Caraka, bestows strength, nourishment, virility, and longevity. 122.
Regarding the powder of *sarpagandhā* (in the *Raktacāpa*):
finely powdered *sarpagandhā* that has been purified by means of a bladder, having prepared it mixed with ghee in a dose of one or two *māṣakas*. ||123||
One afflicted by the disease of insanity (unmāda) should consume it every day, both morning and evening;
through this, sleep arises, which is supremely beneficial for insanity. 124.
This powder of sarpagandhā will undoubtedly act quickly; by means of this, even a mass of blood will certainly be diminished. 125.
"Having repeatedly examined many patients, this has been stated by the royal physician, Śāstrin Īśvaradatta. (126)
Regarding the decoction of *copacīnyā* and others (for blood disorders):
three parts of *copacīnyā*, two parts of *uśavā*, and four parts of sweet *surañjāna* should be taken. (127)
Of *cirātikta*, *gorakṣamuṇḍā*, *dhātrīphala*, *madhuka*, *tiktā*, and *śārivā*, [one should take] each separately. 128.
One part [of sugar] and likewise four parts of grapes—having combined all this together, the physician should store it with care. (129)
This well-known decoction, known as the Upacīnyādi-kaṣāya, is beneficial in all disorders of the blood and effects purification of the digestive tract (koṣṭha). 130.
Then, having taken one tola or two tolas of the substance to be boiled,
one should cook it in water eight times its quantity.
Having removed that decoction when reduced to one-quarter, one should strain it;
once it has cooled, one should add an excellent amount of honey to it. (132)
In cases of blood disorders, the physician should administer this especially;
thus it has been proclaimed by the physician Śrī Rājeśvaradatta. 133.
In the case of pūyameha,
one part of candanādivaṭī and three parts of oil derived from sandalwood, mixed with honey, should be taken in succession by groups of skilled physicians. (134)
Then, having melted beeswax in the fire with a clean cloth and purified it, one should place there oil produced from sandalwood. 135.
Having combined them, one should stir with a ladle until they reach a thick consistency;
once thickened, auspicious pills weighing two ratis each should be prepared. (136)

This pill of sandalwood, renowned for its fragrance, should be constantly attended to by physicians desiring to extract the pus and the urinary disease, just as one would attend to a sandalwood tree. 137.
One or two pills of this [medicine] per day, taken with a decoction of gokṣura for two or three days, is the dosage approved by physicians. (138)
This has been experienced almost always by the learned in Āyurveda;
therefore, out of compassion for the welfare of the world, it has been revealed. 139.

The powder of *balya*, the fruit of *bbūlaja*, *abdhiśoṣa*, and the substances belonging to the group of eight (*aṣṭavarga*) should be taken individually; in their absence, they may be used as prescribed [in the texts]. (140)
The best of physicians should use substances that serve as substitutes for those [original drugs], namely:
śālibāhva, sugar, and the excellent root of the śālmali tree. 141.
Tṛṇakānta, the seed of sūkṣmailā, kattīraka, as well as śvetā and muśalī—each of these should be taken in one part. ||142||
A small amount of cow-dung seed-husk, measured at one-fourth part, is auspicious;
having ground everything finely, it should be mixed with sugar equal in quantity to the entire powder. 143.
In that case, the physician should administer a dose of two māṣas, followed by cow's milk or cold water as a post-drink. ||144||
This powder for strengthening the body quickly removes, especially, excessive volatility of the vital energy (vīrya) and certainly makes it firm. 145.
Now, at the Ayurvedic College of the Viśvavidyālaya, there is a great assembly of fears arising from dreams and urinary disorders. (146)
This has been experienced by the Caraka-teacher Cuñcu Śrīśāstrirājeśvara at all times; let the best of physicians apply it accordingly. 147.
In the case of *tāmreśvaravaṭī* (for the disease of the spleen):
equal parts of asafoetida, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), the leaf of *apāmārga*, the leaf of *arka*, and the leaf of *snuhī* [are to be taken]. (148)
One should take an equal amount of rock salt (saindhava), along with an equal amount of iron and copper;
[this cures] splenomegaly, liver disease, abdominal tumors, and most severe rheumatism (āmavāta). 149.
It cures hemorrhoids, severe abdominal diseases, fainting, jaundice, chlorosis, malabsorption syndrome, diarrhea, consumption, and edema as well. (150)
The Alkaline Pill (for swelling):
there should be two types of alkali, the five salts,
the four [types of] salt, iron, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and the three fruits (phalatrika).
Long pepper root, viḍaṅga pith, mustā, ajamodā, devadāru, and bilva; ||151||
Kaliṅgaka, the root of citraka, pāṭhā, yaṣṭimadhu, ativiṣā, and palāśa— these, along with one karṣa of hiṅgu, should be ground into an extremely fine powder.
Likewise, one drona each of radish and ginger. ||152||
That ash should be prepared with water and stirred until it becomes a thick, non-foaming mass;
then, having formed a dose the size of a jujube fruit and dried it according to the prescribed method, one should employ it. 153.
It cures splenic enlargement, vitiligo, halīmaka, piles, diseases of the feet, anorexia, edema, consumption,
choleraic vomiting, abdominal tumors, artificial poisons, and urinary stones.
It expels asthma and cough, along with kuṣṭha. ||154||
Sauvarcala, saindhava, viḍa, audbhida, and sāmudra salt—here, water should be eight times their quantity. (155)
Regarding *asthisaṃhāra-taila* (for *abhivāta*):
one should take an excellent paste (*kalka*) produced from *asthisaṃhāra* measuring one *kuḍava*, four *prasthas* of its fresh juice (*svarasa*), and one *prastha* of sesame oil. (156)
Having gathered everything together in one place, the physician who knows the procedure for cooking oil should cook it; once the oil is fully prepared, he should set it aside. ||157||
This supreme *asthisaṃhāra-taila* is indeed the pacifier of pain born from trauma; it is highly esteemed by the illustrious Rājeśvara. 158.
The ointment of *kauśika* and others (for ulcers): two parts each of honey and beeswax, and separately, equal parts of oil and resin (*sarjarasa*), are to be taken. (159)
One part and likewise two parts of śrīveṣṭaka;
having taken all of this together, one should first heat the oil. 160.
One should mix guggulu, all the juices, honey, and beeswax;
then, having recognized that they have become one, one should separate them from the fire. ||161||
Having mixed it with fragrant resin (śrīveṣṭaka), one should purify it with a cloth;
then, having placed it in a glass vessel, one should preserve it with every effort. ||162||
For the purpose of increasing the cleansing power, oil derived from mustard seeds should be given;
for the purpose of increasing the healing power, ghee should especially be administered. (164)
A plaster for burnt ulcers consists of linseed oil, resin of the Sarja tree,
and Nimba leaves, taken in portions of four, one, and half [parts] respectively. (165)
First, having taken neem leaves and ground them into a paste according to the prescribed method, one should cook them in linseed oil; then, once it is cooked, one should remove it from the heat.
Then, having filtered the oil through a cloth, one should heat it again and mix it with the powder of *sardana* resin according to the proper method. (167)
One should cook it over a mild fire until it is no longer mixed;
then, having strained it through cloth, one should let it cool. 158.
One should wash that [ointment] one hundred and one times with water;
through the friction with the water, the thick application will then become white. ||169||
This plaster of *itayata* and other ingredients is beneficial for a smeared wound;
it was experienced and described in many ways by Śrī Rājeśvaradatta. 170.

The heartwood of the Udumbara (is used for) cleansing and healing wounds, in vātarakta, and in ophthalmia with excessive lacrimation; the leaves of the Udumbara, washed with water, [are used] in the dilation of the anus.
Having taken one *maṇa* [of each], one should throw them into four times as much water. ||171||
Having boiled it according to the method of decoction, one should reduce it to a quarter part and then dry it; having removed it from the heat, one should then strain it through a cloth. 172.
Furthermore, the physician should cook the decoction until it reaches a state of density;
when it becomes capable of being smeared with a ladle, then he should remove it from the fire. (173)
Having placed it on the steam-engine and stirring it constantly with a ladle, one should cook it skillfully in such a way that it does not burn. (174)
Having ascertained its suitability for the preparation of pills, one should extract it;
then, one should add camphor powder measuring five *tolakas*. (175)
Having cast those ingredients therein and thoroughly mixed them, the physician should preserve that preparation with great care;
this is known by the name Udumbarasāra, composed by the most excellent jewel among physicians. 176.
The one named Śrīcandraśekhara, having appeared on earth, [cures] vātarakta as well as ophthalmia, eye ulcers, and other such ailments. 177.
It destroys various diseases; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
To understand its specific qualities, let them look at the book. 178.
Mixing with water this renowned substance marked by the name "Gūlaraguṇavikāsa," one should fully carry out its application. 179.
For the treatment of *nīḍīvraṇa* (nidivraṇa),
one should take eight hundred and forty *tolakas* of honey, beeswax, and oil,
along with two *tolakas* each of purified mercury, sulfur, and *kajjalī*. (180)
The amount of powder from pure clay, wood, or horn is measured by a *dṛkcolaka*; likewise, that of *kampillaka* is eight *tolakas*. (181)
The physician, having taken one *māṣa* less than three [parts] of purified *tuttha* and having ground it into powder, should collect it all together and grind it diligently in a mortar. (182)
One should mix it with beeswax and oil and store it in a glass vessel;
this is renowned as the impurity-remover known by the name Kajjalikodaya. 183.
Likewise, it is proclaimed to be a purifier and a healer of ulcers;
it has also been experienced by the best of physicians as beneficial even in the case of sinus ulcers (nāḍīvraṇa). ||184||
For visphoṭa (a minor disease),
two *la* of mercury (*sūta*) combined with camphor and the three aromatics (*trisugandha*), along with decoctions of *guḍūcī*, *nimba*, *khadira*, and *indrayava*, [should be applied]. (185)
It would swiftly destroy the boils, just as a wind destroys those who carry away their vigor.
For the *masūrikā-haravaṭī* (pill for smallpox), one should take ten *karṣa*s of the root of *kaṇṭakārī*, and half that amount of black pepper;
then, one should grind these two together into a powder. (187)

Having prepared twenty-one auspicious pills, each the size of a black pepper, by impregnating them with the juice of nimba leaves according to the prescribed method, the physician [should administer them]. (188)
Having dried them in the shade, one should place them in a glass jar;
this is the pill named Masūrikāhara, which cures Adhimasūrika. ||189||
"One or two *vaṭa* fruits should be consumed with water by one desiring one's own welfare";
thus spoke the wise Uśaradatta himself, the elder brother of physicians. 190.
*Devakusumādivaṭī* (for use as an adjunct in food or as an aphrodisiac):
Take *devakusuma*, black pepper, liquid camphor, red sandalwood, saffron, and nutmeg, all in equal parts. (191)

Having ground it in the middle of a mortar, the physician should rub it with lime juice; thereafter, having carefully prepared pills of the measure of a rakti, he should preserve them with diligence. 192.
This pill is renowned in the world by the name Devakusumādivaṭī;
it should be known as the most beneficial pill for use with side dishes (upadaṃśa) and for aphrodisiac purposes (vājīkaraṇa). ||193||
Whoever eats one or two *vaṭa* fruits daily with milk in the morning and evening will certainly become free from disease and happy. (194)
For the pill that destroys ringworm (in the case of *dadru-rogā*):
one should take sulphur, borax, Persian barley (*pārasīkayavānikā*), camphor, and resin of the *sarja* tree, and having taken all these together, grind them into a fine powder. (195)
Having ground it together with water to form pills the size of a single māṣa bean, one should prepare them, dry them in the shade, and then store them. 196.
Having rubbed with water or with the fresh juice of a lime the pill named Dadrughnī, which destroys the pride of ringworm, ||197||
However, the best of physicians should apply that ointment to the site of the skin eruption;
herein is revealed the opinion of Śrī Rājeśvaradatta. 198.
For the medicinal liquid for ringworm (pāmāroga):
take one part each of sulfur, fresh butter, and lime powder, and sixteen parts of water. (199)
Having powdered the sulphur as well, one should combine everything together;
then, having performed the cooking of all the ingredients, one should recognize when it has attained the color of a conch shell. ||200||
Having removed it with a cloth, the physician should purify that [wound];
this liquid sulphur, known by the name Gandhakadrava, is used for skin disorders such as scabies (pāmā) and the like. ||201||
This has been frequently observed by physicians and spoken [by them];
thus it was spoken by Vaidyaka-vid-rāja Īśvaradatta. ||202||
The plaster for ringworm (pāmā):
mercury, sulfur, orpiment, cinnabar, realgar, red ochre, rhinoceros horn, blue vitriol, *vāgujī*, and black pepper. (203)
Having taken these in equal proportions, the physician should grind them finely;
then, he should place them into cow's ghee that has been washed a hundred times and is fourteen times the quantity [of the powder]. (204)
Having mixed the powder, one should grind it for three days in an iron mortar;
this ointment for skin diseases (pāmā) is supreme in removing pāmā. ||205||
This was experienced by Rājeśvara and graciously revealed by the physician Śāstrin to the multitude of those afflicted with the disease of scabies. 206.
A medicinal paste for ringworm (pāmā):
mercury, cinnabar, vermilion, black pepper, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric and *dāru-haridrā*), white cumin, black cumin, sulfur, and realgar. (207)
The best of physicians should take one part of each of these individually;
then, having powdered them all together, one should mix them with cow's ghee. ||208||
This ointment made from the juice and other ingredients is the most excellent remedy for scabies;
this has been personally experienced by Śrī Rājeśvaradatta himself. (209)
For the treatment of leprosy (kuṣṭha),
one should grind one pala of mercury together with five times its amount of iron sulfate (kāsīsa) for the duration of one yāma, using the juice of arjuna bark. 210.
Having sealed it in a pair of earthen saucers, one should indeed cook it using the "kroḍapuṭa" method.
This mercury, bound with kāsīsa (iron sulfate), should be taken with honey in a dose equal to a *vallī* (creeper). ||211||
When combined with *śāṇa* and *vākucī* and used for three months, it certainly destroys *kilāsa*, and especially *dadru*. ||212||

A plaster for leprosy (in cases of *śvitra* and *kuṣṭha*): Turmeric, the bark from the root of the *āraka* tree, and *vāgujī* in equal parts—having taken all of this and prepared it as a fine powder, [one should apply it]. (213)
The prepared substance, purified with a cloth, should be kept in a copper vessel;
this ointment is the best for removing vitiligo and destroying white spots. ||214||
Then the physician, having ground [the ingredients] with cow urine, or sour gruel, or sugarcane juice, should smear it all around the area affected by vitiligo.

And if, at the conclusion of the removal of the plaster, there should be the possibility of burning, then for the sake of preventing that, one should apply oil made from *tuvaraka* and other such substances. (216)
"Āyurveda is to be known as the highest and supreme," thus spoke Bṛhaspati, having experienced it himself out of compassion for King Īśvaradatta. 217.
The Sārivādi decoction (for the purification of blood):
Sārivā, upacīnī, guḍūcī, nimba bark, muṇḍī, kaṭukā, red sandalwood, and harītakī. (218)
This should be taken in equal parts as an excellent, uniform mixture;
having crushed everything together, one should preserve it as a purifier that removes blood. (219)
Having taken two *tolakas* from that [substance] and placed them in pure water sixteen times its quantity, one skilled in decoctions should cause it to boil. 220.
Knowing that only an eighth part remains, one should cause it to descend;
having purified it with a cloth, the one afflicted by disease should drink it with honey. 221.
Indeed, this decoction known as sārivādi is said by the best of physicians to effect the purification of blood and also to bring about the cleansing of the internal organs (koṣṭha). ||222||
Sūtaśekhara-rasa (for acid dyspepsia): In the Sārasaṃgraha, [it is said:
pure mercury, dead gold, ṭaṅkaṇa, vatsanābha [poison], vyoṣa, unmattabīja, sulphur, and copper ash; 223.
One should place equal parts of the four spices (cāturjāta), conch-shell ash, the marrow of the bilva fruit, and kacoraka into a mortar and grind them with *bhṛṅga* juice for one day. 224.
Having made a pill the size of a guñjā seed, one should consume it with honey and ghee;
this elixir destroys acid bile (amlapitta) and removes vomiting and the disease of colic (śūla). 225.

It destroys the five types of gulma and coughs, and is a destroyer of disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī). It cures diarrhea arising from the three doṣas and eliminates dyspnea and weak digestion. 226.
It destroys upward-moving wind (udāvarta), seizures, and hiccups; it removes burning sensations and chronic diseases.
There is no doubt that this Maṇḍala is the supreme remedy for all ailments. 227.
This essence, the crest-jewel of mercurial preparations, is the manifest destroyer of consumption (rājayakṣman);
it is also called by some physicians "the breaker of bile" (pittabhañjī) by name. 228.

For dental plaque (*dantapūya*), collyrium (*añjana*) should be used; likewise, *ākārabhañja*, *coraka*, and that which is known as *candana* (sandalwood), along with *kuṣṭha* and *aśvavacā*—all these taken in equal parts. (229)
The ash produced from the internal smoke of *bhallātaka* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) should be taken in a quantity six times that of all the other powders combined. ||230||
Having mixed all of this together, one should place it in a glass vessel; this collyrium and other preparations bring immediate success for the purpose of cleansing the teeth. 231.
The physicians prescribe an eye-salve called *dantapūyahara* to be used every day in the morning, as well as after eating at night. 232.
According to the opinion of Śrī Rājeśvaradatta, the application of collyrium to the teeth may sometimes be performed even before a meal; this has been made manifest [here]. 233.
An ointment for removing toothache (in cases of dental worms and tooth pain):
rock crystal, the ash of bitter bottle-gourd, long pepper, and the soot produced from the burning of the fruit of *bhallātaka*. (234)
One tola each of all these should be taken separately:
tobacco leaf ash, rock salt, and black pepper. (235)
Ash produced from the bark of the *vātāda* tree, beautiful *krāmuka* ash, and earth-clay from a funeral pyre—each of these should be two *tolakas*. (236)
Having taken all of this together and carefully ground it into a fine powder, one should preserve this excellent collyrium which removes toothache. (237)
In cases of tooth-worms and toothache, it brings incomparable benefit;
this has been experienced by the eminent physicians Rājeśvara and Datta. (238)
In the case of *abhiṣyanda* (an eye disease characterized by excessive lacrimation),
one should use pure, strained water measuring half a *seṭaka*,
along with purified crystal powder, rock salt (*saindhava*), and white sugar candy (*sitopalā*). (239)
Having collected all of that separately and measured it out at four *tolakas*,
one should grind it into a powder and mix it with distilled water.

Having processed these with their juices and dried them, one should grind them into a powder;
