One should mix Musta, mṛgamada, Kṛṣṇā, water, and Candra; this liquid, when combined with these powders measured in śāṇas, becomes as beautiful as Kandarpa. 41.
At night, one should eat a *śaṇa*-measure each of sugar, *dhātrī*, and *vidārikā*, combined with a *karṣa* of ghee and a *karṣa* of the powder of these [same] substances. 42.
Following that, one whose mind is devoted to his friend should drink two palas of milk; he may enjoy many women, yet his virility suffers no loss whatsoever. 43.
The mercury that stabilizes vigor—
take one *śūdra* measure of mercury, one *iṣupratola* measure of sulfur,
and likewise one *śūdrimat* measure of *pañcākṣa*; having taken these, open a conch-shell with its mouth restrained.

Having removed that insect from the interior of the oyster shell, one should place the *kandhaka* inside; then, having applied the prescribed softness (*ārdrava*), all the mercury (*sūta*) should be deposited within it. 44.
Having sprinkled the remaining powder of *gandhaka* over the mercury (*sūta*), one should seal the mercury situated within it using another shell (*śuktikā*) placed on top; then,
having thoroughly dried that shell with clay wrappings, it is ignited by the rays of the sun.

One should grind the grains known as *gaja* (elephant) while they are still warm from their own heat, strain them quickly through a fine cloth, and take one *guñjā* measure of this powder. This promotes nourishment and acts as a semen-stabilizer;
one should drink it with milk mixed with sugar in the evening. ||45||
The medicinal pill of the Sugata consists of mercury, fragrant campaka, keśara, saffron, cloves, and karahāṭa;
as well as goat’s milk, the drying of the ocean, jasmine leaves, and nutmeg. ||46||

One part each of [the aforementioned ingredients] and two parts of pure opium should be taken; with these, a pill the size of a jujube fruit should be made, and one should then consume it with honey. 47.
Having stayed near a woman during the past watch of the night, one should consume half a *taila* (sesame oil) as an attractant for Yama’s attendants; this indeed is its after-drink. 48.
The penis shall become extremely firm, and there shall be retention of semen for a watch (yāma).
This is the Sugata-guṭikā; truly, truly, it is a restrainer of semen. 49.

One *māṣa* of mercury (*sūta*) possessing the essence of Kāmadeva is free from its own defects; one-fourth of that amount is *bali*, and the same measure of *bhuṅga-phaena* is declared [to be used] with the water of *kṣudrā-phala*.
Having prepared this pill, one should cook it in the juice of *kṣudrā-phala* within a crucible (*hemaga*).
With eight parts of salt, this elixir named Śrīkāmadeva is produced. ||50||
At sunrise, one *guñjā* with *mātrā*;
for four watches [of the day], four *guñjās* combined with the juice of betel leaves;
at night, milk-rice with salt, and milk as desired. ||51||
A paste for stiffening virility consists of mercury, zinc, camphor, and an equal amount of munirasa mixed with honey;
having ground these together, one should apply it to the penis and remain so for one watch (yāma). ||52||
Then, having washed it, one hundred women may enjoy the essence of its juice at ease;
this, which causes the retention of semen in men, was correctly proclaimed by Nāgārjuna. 53.
Madanataila is derived from dried earthworms, from pure marking-nut (bhallātaka), from nutmeg,
and from the ākāra-karabha plant. ||54||
One *śāṇa* measure each of the powder made from deer-dust, and two *kuḍava* measures of *āphala* oil should be taken from the wind [element]. (55)
Then, having placed [the substance] in a wide-mouthed glass jar, one should carefully seal its mouth for one month in a well-protected place. (56)
One should preserve it in its place; thereafter, that stainless and excellent oil should be taken by skillful means from the surface—purified and free from dregs. ||57||
By massaging this, the failure of the penis that arises from unrighteous sexual intercourse and the like is destroyed;
of this there is no doubt. (58)
The names of the medicinal plants for aphrodisiacs have been fully declared in the section titled Vājīkaraṇa;
likewise, there are the Svalpacandrodaya and Bṛhaccandrodaya, as well as the Makaradhvaja. 59.
The Siddhasūta, Pañcaśara, and likewise the Kāmadīpaka;
and the Darpaghna rasa, joined with the word "kāminī," is the most excellent. 60.
The flower-bowed god (Kāmadeva) who kindles the fire of passion, the essence (rasa), the full moon, and likewise the Siddha-Śālmalī tree—[these are the five arrows]. ||61||
Such other juices as these, beginning with Trikaṇṭaka and named Śrīmadanānanda, are likewise to be consumed according to the prescribed rule. 62.
Physicians should also prepare modakas and rasālā in well-prepared ghee made from aśvagandhā and amṛtaprāśa. 63.
The oil named Śrīgopāla, the oil called Pallavasāra, and the Mahācandanādi oil should be used with great care. 64.
Such medicinal herbs should always be administered after careful consideration, according to the specific humors involved, in order to bring about the destruction of the disease.

In the event of the breaking of the flag, it is beneficial to consume śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, wheat, lentils, chickpeas, and the like; as well as fresh butter, milk, liquor, rum, and the vartaka bird. ||66||
The flesh of the sparrow, the cock, the partridge, the deer, as well as that of the hare and the goat—these are indeed tender. (67)
The fruits of grapes, dates, mangoes, rose-apples, and pomegranates are declared by the wise to be wholesome in cases of the "falling of the banner" (dhvajabhaṅga). 68.
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of impotence (*dhvajabhaṅga*) within the section on specific diseases in the *Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī*. 92.
Now begins the section on the treatment of kidney diseases (vṛkkaroga), [chapter] 93.
The etiology of kidney disease:
generally, due to the specific application of coldness, kidney disease arises in both kidneys;
it also occurs in cases of smallpox and cholera.
Or rather, [is it] in chronic āmavāta or even in long-standing fever?
That [consciousness] would have taken birth as a state of affliction; this is the opinion of the wise regarding consciousness. ||1||
Specifically, kidney disease arises in the bodies of men due to the transformation of the blood; such is the conclusion of physicians. (2)

Its premonitory symptoms are loss of sleep and diminished digestive fire; in kidney disease (vṛkkaroga), swelling of the eyes and face, stiffness of the vessels, and a sensation of heat and dryness are declared to be the premonitory signs. ||3||
Regarding the nature of the kidneys during a state of disease: when the pair of kidneys is afflicted by illness, they certainly become enlarged as well as soft.
Furthermore, a doubling of the size and a swelling of the veins are also observed there in the middle of the eye. ||4||
Even for a liquid situated within a channel, there is a great accumulation;
likewise, there is a supreme excretion from the kalā that holds the urine.
Its symptoms are vomiting, swelling, and pain in all the limbs, as well as headache, fever,
and a pale complexion in the face due to the discharge of blood through the nose.
In cases of absence of perspiration due to dryness of the body and sluggish digestion, there is pain in the waist, the abdomen, and the region of the kidneys;
furthermore, the pulse will certainly become forceful. ||6||
In kidney disease (vṛkkaroga), urine flows constantly in the form of drops, being hot and accompanied by pain;
such intense symptoms likewise arise in both kidneys even due to the presence of urinary calculi (aśmarī). ||7||
Excessive pain arises at the tip of the penis,
and the urine may occasionally be mixed with blood; moreover,
the hands and feet become cold, while there is slight burning at the glans penis during urination.
When the two kidneys are affected due to the slackening of bodily functions, the disease is characterized by various severe and subtle symptoms;
the signs of a disease involving the spleen, heart, liver, and kidneys have been thus described. Furthermore, there is ringing in the ears, eye disease, and disorders arising in the penis.
Breaking pain, a sense of sinking as if into a whirlpool, fainting, and intense pressure in the shoulders, neck, and head—
these are the symptoms of delusion (moha). ||10||

The complications [of poisoning by urine] are fainting, cough, edema of the lung tissue, as well as *arastoya* (blood-stained sputum), hydrothorax, and likewise ascites; furthermore, there is the internal movement of the poison through the urine. ||11||
Indeed, these complications arise specifically as diseases of the kidneys. ||12||
The physician must first perform the course of treatment after due deliberation according to the rules;
[he must consider] bloodletting, as well as the relative strength and weakness of the patient and the disease. (13)
Then, one should employ purgation, sudation, as well as excellent diuretics, along with diet, drinks, and medicine, in the treatment of kidney disease. 14.
When a severe obstruction of disease has arisen, an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) is beneficial;
however, it should be avoided from afar by those who know the science of life—this is the opinion of the experts. 15.
When constipation of feces has occurred, an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) is beneficial;
in cases of renal calculus (vṛkkāśmaryā), the entire therapeutic sequence is pleasant and removes the stone. 16.
One should prepare a pill weighing one *rakti* by grinding together gold, silver, mica, iron, lac, sulphur, and honey, using the juice of *varuṇa* as the medium. (17)
This Vaṭī, known as Sarvatobhadrā, removes all diseases arising from the kidneys and those originating in the bladder;
it also increases strength and virility. (18)
Māheśvaravaṭī,
gaganam, kāntaloha, crystal, gold, pearl,
the root of sahadevī, and kṣīrapuṣpī— all these in equal parts. (19)
Having powdered white *varṣābhū*, *gokṣura*, and dried radish, one should saturate [the powder] seven times with their decoctions separately according to the prescribed method. 20.
Virtuous physicians should prepare pills measuring two guñjās each;
by the consumption of this pill named Māheśvarī, [the desired result] is certainly attained. 21.
[It cures] kidney disease, dropsy, anemia, as well as irregular fever and swelling arisen throughout the entire body. ||22||
One should quickly dispel fainting just as a thunderbolt fells trees;
milk-rice should be diligently consumed because it is wholesome in nature. 23.
One should employ here the medicinal substances mentioned in the section on rejuvenation (rasāyana);
for there is no specific medicine prescribed for its pacification. 24.

Having carefully considered, in particular, the time, the strength, and the specific condition of the patients, the physician should cause them to take these wholesome, strengthening, and easily digestible foods. 25.
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of kidney diseases within the section on specific disorders in the Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī. 93.
Now begins the chapter on the treatment of afflictions and diseases. 94.
First, regarding the nature of the *kloma*:
that which is currently known by modern physicians as the "seat of fire" (*agnyāśaya*) is what is designated by the term *kloma*.
Where, then, is the *kloma* as prescribed by the ancient physicians?
For even now, that which is called the *kloman* has not been definitively determined.
The specific nature of the *kloman* is now described according to modern [anatomical] understanding:
it is located on the right side, below the heart.
According to the opinion of the learned, its abode is the liver. ||2||

This speech, however, is surely a unique root of a flowing stream of water; it is especially characterized by the production of thirst, having been repeatedly observed by groups of those ignorant of the waters of existence. (3)

The etiology of kidney disease (kloma-roga) is as follows: an increase in exhaustion, or alternatively, softness [of the tissues], resulting from the excessive consumption of unctuous or very heavy foods.
Or rather, is it surely produced within the human body solely through blows and the like? ||4||

Furthermore, although a collection of weapons may be seen joined together here, an abscess (vidradhi) certainly arises from such causes in many ways; likewise, through improper channels, they become exceedingly painful. ||5||

The symptoms of kidney disease (kloma-roga) are a decrease in digestive fire, pallor, emaciation, vertigo, and exhaustion; furthermore, these occur in the case of upward displacement of the abdomen (ūrdhva-udara).
In a disease located in the kloma, there is heat, hardness, nausea, vomiting, and jaundice as well.
When the swelling has matured, there occurs pain and distension in this abscess;
moreover, there is excessive thirst, and a most terrible stone-like formation resembling a urinary calculus (aśmarī) inevitably causes great suffering. ||7||
Regarding the treatment of disease of the kloman:

that which is said to kindle the digestive fire, namely dhanvayavāsa (dhanyāka) and viśvabheṣaja (śuṇṭhī), as well as all food, drink, and medicine—each of these is beneficial for the disease of the kloman. 8.
A decoction of Abhayā, Āmalaka, Dāru, Dhanyāka, Viśvabheṣaja, Drākṣā,
and Śārivā removes diseases of the kloma. (9)
Surendramodaka, Śrīsaṃjñā, Bhaṅgurā, Śyāmā, Abjamūla,
Pīvarī, Dīpyakā, Capalā, Śṛṅgī, Drākṣā, Chatrā, and Harītakī. ||10||
The physician should prepare boluses (modakas) by crushing [the ingredients] with honey;
one should consume them according to one's strength for the destruction of diseases of the kloma. 11.
This modaka, known as Surendra, promotes nourishment, increases strength, kindles the digestive fire, is pleasing to the heart, and is considered the best among elixirs (rasāyana). ||12||
The mercury of Śaśiśekhara, along with mercury, sulphur, mica, gold, coral, and pearl,
when rubbed for three days and nights, becomes a "licked" (lidva) rasa. 13.
The best of physicians should determine its dose to be one guñjā;
one should habitually consume this juice with honey along with the decoctions of kloman, heartwood, and aged substances. 14.
By that, all diseases of the kloma, as well as those arising from wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha), are quickly and completely destroyed without exception. ||15||
Surendrābhra, vaṭī,
and abhra burnt a thousand times, mercury extracted from darada,
sulphur purified with the juices of the king of plants (reśarāja), and diamond; ||16||
Having ground together gold, coral, pearl, silver, honey, and iron, according to the prescribed method with fire and water; 17.
Vallisneria roots, measured at one valla and dried in the shade, should be consumed with great care, accompanied by appropriate after-drinks according to the specific dosha. 18.
For the destruction of kidney diseases and for the kindling of the digestive fire, [it cures] acid bile, liver swelling, spleen disorders, anemia, and ascites. 19.
It destroys abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, and severe irregular fevers, as well as most dreadful leprosy; of this there is no doubt. ||20||
Whichever disease may affect the kloman, the physician, having examined each one, should successfully apply the treatment according to the specific humor involved and the patient's strength. ||21||
One afflicted by *kloma* should consume wholesome and unwholesome food and drink as prescribed,
yet one must always and with great effort strictly avoid that which is harmful. 22.
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of *kloma* disease within the section on specific diseases in the *Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī*. (94)
Now begins the section on the treatment of syphilis (phiraṅgaroga).
Regarding that, the etymology of the word *phiraṅga* is as follows: because it occurs predominantly in the country known by the name *phiraṅga*.
Therefore, this disease has been called "Phiraṅga" by those expert in the science of pathology. ||1||

The remote cause of syphilis is the disease of the gandha; this syphilis certainly arises in embodied beings from contact with the body of a syphilitic person or through association with a syphilitic woman. (2)
For this disease is indeed exogenous; here, there is a transference of the humors (doṣas). The best of physicians should observe it through their respective symptoms. ||3||
The disease known as phiraṅga is to be understood as being of three types: external, internal, and that which arises from both outside and within;
I shall now describe their symptoms.
Among those, the external [type] is the *phiraṅga* (syphilis), which resembles a *visphoṭa* (boil) and has little pain;
it is known to be easily curable once it has burst and is recognized as a wound. ||5||
Located within the joints, it causes pain like that of āmavāta and produces swelling;
this is considered by the wise to be difficult to cure.
Emaciation, loss of strength, nasal obstruction, dullness of the digestive fire,
wasting of the bones, and curvature of the bones— these are the complications of syphilis (phiraṅga). (7)
The foreign [syphilis] may be curable;
its manifestation is new and free from complications.
However, this internal disease is difficult to cure. (8)

The sages of old said that a disease which has entered deep within, is chronic, is accompanied by complications in one who is already weakened, and has reached an incurable state, is indeed "Ayah" (Iron/Incurable). 9.
Now, the treatment for syphilis (phiraṅgaroga). Regarding the method of consuming camphor-mercury (karpūrarasa):
mercury known as "camphor" [cures] the disease known as syphilis.
"The physicians of old have said that this will certainly cause destruction. ||10||
The supreme procedure for the consumption of mercury-camphor is now being written.
By this procedure, one should eat it, and swelling shall not afflict the mouth. 11.
Having kneaded wheat flour, the physician should fashion a small cup;
he should then place mercury, measured at four guñjās, into its interior. (12)
Then one should make a pill such that it is not visible on the outside;
one should dust that bolus with the fine powder of cloves. 13.
One should swallow it with water in such a way that there is no contact with the teeth; likewise, one should avoid fatigue, heat, travel, and especially sexual intercourse. (14)
Seven śāli-weights shall constitute one pārada; it shall be equal to eight ṭaṅkas of khadira;
and the ākāra-karabha is also to be taken as measured by two ṭaṅkas. ||15||
The physician should place three ṭaṅkas of honey into a mortar, grind all of it together, and prepare seven pills from the entire mixture. ||16||
The patient, however, should consume one pill with water every morning; he must avoid sour and salty foods, and his syphilis (phiraṅga) will be destroyed. ||17||

For the application of smoke, there should be one karṣa of mercury and exactly the same amount of sulphur; the rice grains should be one akṣa in measure. One should prepare a collyrium from these. 18.
One should prepare seven pills from that [substance] and apply its smoke for seven days; by that means, the end of the Phiranga disease will come, without a doubt. (19)
One should rub the mercury, measured by one iṣṭaṅka, with the juice of yellow flowers, bala, and leaves, using both hands until the mercury is no longer visible. (20)
Then one should cause the patient to sweat in this manner for seven days;
he should avoid salt and sour things, and his syphilis will perish.
One should powder neem leaves with one-eighth part of harītakī; likewise, āmalakī should be an equal portion, and neem [powder] should be one-sixteenth part by weight for one night.
One should consume this powder, measured by a śāṇa, along with water;
it certainly destroys syphilis (phiraṅga), both external and internal. ||23||
One should consume one *śāṇa* measure of powder derived from *copacīnī* mixed with honey for the destruction of the disease of syphilis (*phiraṅga*), and one should avoid salt. 24.
If a person is unable to renounce salt entirely, then they should consume rock salt (saindhava), which is exceedingly sweet and beneficial. 25.
One karṣa of mercury,
one karṣa of sulphur,
and one karṣa of khadira— these should be made into a kajjalī (a black collyrium-like paste). 26.
Rajanī, keśara, the two types of truṭi, the two types of jīra, yavānikā, the two types of candana, kṛṣṇā, vāṃśī, māṃsī, and patrakam. ||27||
Having powdered all of that, measuring half a karṣa, one should mix it with honey and ghee, two palas each, separately. 28.
Then a person should rub it and consume one karṣa of that;
the ulcer arising from diseases such as phiraṅga will certainly be destroyed. ||29||
Even a great ulcer, though it has been present for three years, is pacified;
by consuming this, swelling does not arise within the mouth. (30)
One should avoid salt here for twenty-one days. ||31||
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of syphilis within the section on specific diseases in the *Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī*. 95.
Now begins the section on the treatment of diseases of the ligaments (snāyu). 96.
Regarding that, the etiology and symptoms of Snāyukaroga (ligament disease) are as follows: Aggravated [by the doshas], it produces swelling in the extremities like erysipelas (visarpa);
having burst that [swelling] at the site of injury, it dries up the flesh along with its heat. ||1||
One should make a thread resembling a fiber from those lumps made of buttermilk and barley flour;
by cutting it very slowly, starting from a wound, it brings about its destruction. ||2||
From its falling, there is subsidence of the swelling, but it may recur in another location;
this is known as snāyu, and the treatment prescribed here is the same as for visarpa.
If, through negligence, it should break on the arms or even on the shanks, it certainly causes contraction and lameness when severed. (4)

For the treatment of diseases of the ligaments (snāyuka), one should perform appropriate procedures such as oleation (sneha), sudation (sveda), and emesis (pralopa). Asafoetida (rāmaṭha) drunk with cold water cures the disease of the ligaments. ||5||
Just as a frog prepared with sour gruel (kāñjika) causes intense sweating when applied,
so too does the seed of the babūla tree, ground into a paste, destroy [the effects of poison] through application.
Having drunk cow’s urine for three days and the fresh juice of nirguṇḍī for three days, one will certainly destroy even the most virulent snāyuka disease; of this there is no doubt. (7)

The root of *suṣavī* ground with snow-water, when drunk, quickly brings peace to this fierce disease of the tendons (tendonitis) even when accompanied by ulcers in men; having drunk it with *ghṛta* from *aśvagandhā*—it is called *gandharvagandha* because it possesses the fragrance (*gandha*) of a *gandharva*, namely *aśvagandhā*—[the same result is achieved]. ||8||
This powder—consisting of ativisa, mustaka, bhārgī, viśvauṣadha, pippalī, and bibhītaka—destroys seminal threads when drunk by men with warm water. (9)
An ointment made from ground roots and leaves of the śigru plant mixed with sour gruel (kāñjika) and rock salt is considered the supreme remedy for the disease of the sinews (snāyuka). ||10||
By carefully applying a plaster made from the root of *ahiṃsrā* ground with water, the arrow will not emerge from its binding; of this there is no doubt. (11)
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of Snāyukaroga (nerve diseases) within the section on specific diseases in the Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī. ||96||
Now begins the chapter on the medical treatment of the transformations of mercury (pārada). 97.
When mercury becomes free from defects,
it is indeed remembered as the remover of old age and death;
therefore, it is pure and resembles nectar.
Poison is specifically declared to be impure. ||1||
Flavor improperly applied is the root of disease; flavor properly applied is the thorn of old age and sickness.
Since it has been thus prescribed by distinguished physicians, it should therefore be consumed according to rule by those who possess expert knowledge. ||2||
Indeed, this elixir, when consumed according to the prescribed rules, surely removes all diseases from men;
yet, if it is consumed improperly, it indeed produces these various ailments upon the earth. (3)

Deformity of the nose, chronic rhinitis, loss of teeth, various diseases arising in the eyes and mouth, erysipelas, skin eruptions, itching, excessive pain in the head, discoloration of the skin, and wounds on the nose and other parts [occur]. (4)
Painful nodules, swelling, and hardness arise in both testicles;
there may also be hemiplegia, nodular wind, stiffness of the bones, severe burning, and even mental derangement. (5)

Fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, the various types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and the symptoms of venereal sores (upadaṃśa) in the middle of the body—as well as other most difficult diseases—should be treated here with appropriate medicinal remedies. ||6||
Another set of symptoms indicating the transformation of mercury [into the body] is as follows: the gums become reddish, soft, swollen, and ulcerated;
there is pain like that of being pricked by needles, and the presence of many cavities. (7)
There is filth and looseness of the teeth, as well as the trickling of saliva from the mouth;
moreover, the taste of metallic minerals therein is utterly unpleasant. (8)
Swelling, inflammation, likewise tearing, emaciation of the body, and the onset of diseases such as galashuṇḍī (tonsillitis) and others [arise]. ||9||
Swelling in the throat, at the root of the ears, and in the jaw also arise;
these signs are constantly present in the disorder of the menstrual blood (sūta-vikṛti). ||10||
If that mercury (pārada) is consumed excessively and without interruption, then it causes depression of the mind, fever, and even physical weakness. ||11||
It certainly causes the falling out of teeth, the decay of the bones of the jaw, as well as abscesses in the mouth, internal hemorrhaging, and jaundice. ||12||
Thus, generally causing men to produce such diseases and the like, he will very swiftly lead them at the end into the presence of the Ender (Antaka). 13.
The symptoms of the agitation caused by the speed of the mercury's vapor arise from the excessive inhalation of the vapors produced by the mercury;
beginning with trembling of the face, it spreads down to the arms and legs. (14)
In men, there arises an extreme weakness of the muscles, as well as a disorder of the functioning of the sense organs and a general decline. ||15||
The symptoms of the transformation of the quick-acting poison (sūta) include swelling accompanied by pain in the middle of the internal viscera (adhyāmāśaya),
and death occurs once the disease has reached its final stage in the patient.
Diarrhea accompanied by blood, vomiting, and even fainting [arise]. ||16||
"The characteristic of a disorder arising from a swift-acting poison has been experienced by the physician and revealed in its entirety through the [medical] treatises. (17)
Regarding the treatment for the transformation of mercury:
one should consume a dose of four *raktis* every day;
apart from pure sulfur (*gandha*), there is no medicine whatsoever that is superior. (18)
It destroys all modifications of the vital breath and brings about the true complexion of the body. ||19||
A decoction made from Triphalā, Kaṭukā, Bhīru, Paṭola, Amṛta, and Parpaṭa,
when drunk or applied externally, removes the disorders arising from mercury (sūta). 20.
The decoction of bitter and other herbs consists of Tiktā, Amṛtā, Anantā, Mahāśrāvaṇikā,
Varī, Pathyā, Gopavadhū, Vāyasī, and Duṣparadharṣiṇī. ||21||
The physician should boil equal parts of jīvanī, śrīphala, and dhātrīphala, and then apply that decoction to the disease produced by mercury (sūta). 22.
Śārivādyavaleha:
One should boil one *tulā* (ten *prasthas*) of *śārivā* in one *droṇa* of water;
when the decoction is reduced to one-fourth, [one should add] *varī*, *tiktā*, *amṛtā*, and *varā*. (23)
Trivṛt, the group of life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, upakuñcikā, and trāyantī—each of these, powdered, in the measure of two akṣas. ||24||
Having added these, it should be prepared like a linctus according to the prescribed rules by the best of physicians;
one should then pour into it eight palas of honey when it has cooled. ||25||
One should then consume a quantity of one karṣa with milk as a vehicle;
by the mere use of this, diseases arising from blood disorders [are cured]. (26)
Pustules, as well as upadaṃśa and the twenty types of prameha—all these disorders arising from sūka are certainly specific [to this condition]. 27.
All diseases perish, as do other [afflictions], and moreover, the human being becomes endowed with strength, complexion, and digestive fire, and shall be constantly happy. (28)
Seeing a man afflicted by thirst and suffering from disorders of the vital fluids (sūta),
the physician should immediately give him coconut water to drink.

Whatever excellent medicine has been prescribed for fainting (mūrchā) and epilepsy (apasmāra), the physician should employ all of that here according to the specific dosha involved. ||18||
One should eliminate all defects of the bowstring according to the prescribed rules;
a woman suffering from *apatantaka* (prolapse) should be cured through soothing words and the giving of what is dear to her. ||19||
Two parts each of the essence of Bhūtabhairava (the *bṛhat* [form]), gold ash, and golden vermilion, along with pearl, coral,
and beautiful iron filings, separately. 20.
One part of this should be taken and ground with the water of a virgin girl and also with the juice produced from *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, according to the prescribed rite.
Having wrapped it for three days with the leaves of the *gandharvahasta* plant, one should place that ball (*golaka*) upon a heap of grain according to the prescribed method. 22.
Then, having extracted from that [substance] a pill the size of a stalk of barley, one should practice with a single pill combined with excellent sugar. 23.
Alternatively, this auspicious lake, Bṛhadbhūtabhairava, when combined with milk, destroys the madness caused by spirits. ||24||
The woman quickly [contracted] the terrible apatantraka, as well as epilepsy, intoxication, fainting, and various pains arising from wind (vāta). ||25||
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of women suffering from incontinence, within the section on specific diseases in the Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī. 103.
Now begins the section on the treatment of itching of the female genital tract (yoni-kaṇḍū-cikitsā-prakaraṇam), chapter 104.
The cause of that [condition] is generally due to a disorder of the phlegm (śleṣman) in the womb, which provokes hemorrhoids; it also occurs when a tumor arises in the bladder,
or from the dilation of the vessels located in the region of the vagina.
Or rather, what is more wretched than the decay of women? ||1||
Due to constant excessive indulgence with a man, and because the menstrual period has generally set in,
an itching arises within the middle of the vagina caused by the provocation of Vata before the conception of the fetus. (2)
Thus, the physicians have described the etiology of vaginal itching, specifically due to the increase of female reproductive fluids. ||3||
The characteristics of *yonikaṇḍūla* (vaginal itching): when there is itching in the vagina, it is *yonikaṇḍū*; there will certainly be pricking pain, roughness, and dryness as well.
In this world, the increase of a disease is declared by the best of physicians to result from heat, while its pacification results from cold.

Its treatment consists of administering unctuous purification for vaginal itching, diseases, and the like; furthermore, one should employ strengthening, rejuvenating (rasāyana) medicine, and remedies that remove defects of the blood. (5)
One should cause a decoction of the two types of sārivā, trivṛt, lodhra,
and gajapippalī to be drunk by a woman afflicted with itching and pain in the vagina.
One should prepare auspicious pills (śubhakarī vaṭī) by grinding equal parts of opium, the essence of nectar (kāmamṛtasāra), iron pyrite,
and musta with alkaline water (analanīra), and then forming them into pills weighing one māṣa each. ||7||
This auspicious pill instantly destroys itching and skin lesions. ||8||
The powder of śilājatu and other ingredients:
śilājatu, saubhāgya, vāṃśī, the five salts, anala, padmaka, blue lotus (nīlotpala), dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and mustaka. ||9||
Having powdered grapes, guduchi, jivanti, madhuka, and the two types of sandalwood, one should have a woman drink it with water for the pacification of itching. 10.

When itching occurs within the vagina, one should apply cold water sprinklings, oleation, sudation, and the enema known as *uttara-basti*; furthermore, all the medicinal remedies previously mentioned for gynecological disorders (yonivyāpad) are beneficial. 11.

Whatever food and drink is wholesome or unwholesome, which facilitates the downward movement of wind (vāta), is easily digested, and kindles the digestive fire—that should be consumed; the rest should be avoided with effort. 12.
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of vaginal itching (yonikaṇḍū) within the section on specific diseases in the Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī. 104.
Now begins the chapter on the treatment of diseases of the seminal receptacle (aṇḍādhāra), [numbered] 105.
The cause of this disease is excessive sexual indulgence, exposure to extreme cold, as well as physical trauma, the consumption of poison, and the eating of unwholesome food;
thus the disorder known as *aṇḍādhāra* (scrotal enlargement) arises constantly among women. ||1||
Its symptoms are: pain in the thighs, distension of the abdomen, difficulty in passing urine, scanty urine, and blood in the urine;
furthermore, loss of appetite, restlessness, loss of strength, fever, and nausea arise when this condition occurs. ||2||
The veins of a woman afflicted by a disorder of the uterus (aṇḍādhāra) are small, throbbing, dilated, crooked, and constantly reddish-bright;
these are the signs to be recognized by physicians—thus it has been well said. ||3||

The treatment for that disease of the testicles is as follows: whatever food and drink provides strength and whatever promotes the downward movement of the Vāta should be administered by the best of physicians. (4)
The decoction of the *paṭolādi* group consists of *paṭola*, *madhuka*, *mūrvā*, *drākṣā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *viḍaṅga*, *balā*, *pītamūlī*,
*dhanyāka*, *rāsnā*, and likewise *indrayava*. (5)

One suffering from diseases residing in the *maṇḍa* (the upper part of the stomach) should boil trijātaka, cloves, two types of *kaṇā* (long pepper), and the two types of *niśā* (turmeric), and drink the resulting water.
Amṛta should be taken with honey; it is beneficial for disorders of the āma, the ādhāra, and fever.
One should prepare pills of the size of a *valla* by processing mercury (which is beloved by women), vermilion, antimony, *vaikrānta*, gold, and borax with excellent water. 8.
Like a lion slaying deer, this elixir, when cherished by women, destroys all diseases arising from the womb.
The powder of sandalwood and other ingredients consists of the two types of sandalwood, mūrvā, the two types of blue cardamom,
murā, the two types of long pepper, trivṛt, grapes, māṃsī, madhuka, and mustaka. (10)
Having thoroughly powdered all of that, which destroys the gadā-disease residing in the abdomen, the wielder of the mace (Gadinī), seeking happiness, should drink it daily with warm milk. ||11||
Regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome:
here, the wholesome consists of oblation, milk, śāli rice, aged barley, sesame, and even the broth of goat meat;
however, pungent substances do not lead to well-being. 12.
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of Aṇḍādhāra disease in the *Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī*, within the section on specific diseases, in the vernacular commentary titled *Vidyotinī*. (105)
Now begins the section on the treatment for those wishing to die. 106.
Indeed, one who desires to die by drowning in water or the like, by hanging with a noose or similar means,
or by strangling the throat, is called one who is "about to die" (apamumūrṣu). ||1||
The obstruction of the breath is considered the cause of death through drowning and similar means;
therefore, when the breath is brought under control, a living being lives with effort. (2)
As long as the body is still warm and the limbs are not yet slackened, so long must medical treatment be administered; for generally, death follows at the end of the staff.
In the treatment of one submerged in water, one should skillfully cause a man to lie face down on the back of a pitcher, submerged in water; by this method, the water shall exit from his mouth. 4.
Having lifted the person submerged in water and supported their body by the armpits,
one should expel the water from the mouth and remove the phlegm and saliva.
One should keep the people away from that place so that the wind does not become defiled. ||5||
Regarding the procedure for restoring one whose breath has ceased:
while he lies there, one should forcefully instill a nasal medication (nasya) into his nostrils;
then, one should touch his throat with a finger or with a smooth piece of wood. 6.
By this method, when a fit of sneezing or vomiting occurs during the onset [of the disease], the dyspnea returns and even one who was near death lives. ||7||
By rubbing the face and chest together and applying cold water there, the breath returns;
even one who was near death thus lives. ||8||
If the breath does not thus return, the physician— skilled in his craft and having performed the preliminary procedures—
should perform this treatment in order to initiate the management of the dyspnea.
Having placed the patient lying face down with a pillow beneath his chest,
the physician should then lay him on his side and press down upon both hands.
One should perform this practice within a pala, dividing it into six or seven parts, until the breath no longer enters, or until death is certain. 11.
Having placed a pillow beneath him, one should lay him on his back;
then, one should pull out the tongue, and while pulling it, one should likewise pull the arm oneself. (12)
Sitting near the head, one should perform this rite six or seven times on the abdomen and the chest;
one should continue this practice until breath no longer returns, or until death is certain. ||13||
If the breath still does not enter despite such effort, one should diligently rub the thighs and arms and then apply dry sudation (rūkṣasveda) to the upper body. ||14||
Thus, by all actions and when the breath has proceeded, one lives. ||15||
Then, once he has regained his breath, one should feed him strengthening food and drink, and also have him drink the "reviving-dead" liquor (surā). ||16||

When overcome by the impulse of sleep, he should sleep on a comfortable, well-spread, and auspicious bed; furthermore, the best of physicians should diligently maintain his regimen with wholesome food.
The medical treatment for one wishing to die by hanging is as follows:
a physician skilled in this procedure should treat the patient who has been released from the hanging by means of inducing breath and other such methods. (18)
Having cut the cord around the neck, one should rub it with warm clarified butter;
one should also fan with a palm-leaf fan to ensure the proper passage of flatus. ||19||
Once consciousness has returned, one should administer wholesome substances;
however, until full strength is restored, one should protect the patient from fatigue and other such strains. (20)
One should treat those who have fainted from fear, from falling from a height, or from the heat of a vajra-fire, whether caused by extreme terror or otherwise;
one should treat the one whose consciousness is lost according to the previously mentioned method. (21)

For one scorched by the fire of a thunderbolt, a treatment that is extremely cooling is beneficial; likewise, one who has fallen from a tree or similar height should indeed be treated in this very same way. 22.
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of those about to die, within the section on specific diseases in the Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī. ||106||
Thus, this treasury of the Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī, complete and refined, has been [composed] by Brahman Śaṅkara for the joy of physicians.
